cards.title: Write the Advertorial for One Real Customer, Not a Crowd
cards.summary: Pick a single verified buyer from your ad data and write the advertorial as if it were for them alone, which makes it resonate with many.
cards.use_when: When briefing or drafting an advertorial, pre-lander, listicle or VSL and deciding which customer to write to.
steps: Pull actual ad/order data and identify a buyer who matches the core demographic you want to scale to (e.g. a 72-year-old woman with chronic knee pain).
Mine that person's profile, comment, or send them a short survey to learn the specifics of their situation: age, location, how long they've had the problem, what they've tried.
Write the advertorial as if addressing only that one person — one age, one gender, one problem duration. The presenter's example headline: 'Woman, 72, finally free from knee pain after 3 years'.
Avoid stacking multiple demographics ('if you're 18, 28 or 57, man or woman...') because readers stop feeling spoken to and disengage.
Carry the same persona, hook and promise from the ad creative into the advertorial headline and body, then into the product page — the same person should be visible at every step.
caveats: The presenter's 'write for one customer' device is advice from a health/wellness advertorial writer; survey your own buyer list to keep the persona accurate rather than guessing.
Over-narrowing to an unrepresentative buyer can hurt if your scale audience is much broader.

cards.title: Audit Your Draft for the Moment the Story Stops
cards.summary: Read the advertorial back and flag every sentence where storytelling turns into a sales pitch — those are the tab-close points.
cards.use_when: When editing a finished advertorial or pre-lander before publishing, to find where narrative breaks down.
steps: Read the full draft assuming you are a reader, not the writer.
Highlight every sentence that stops telling the story and starts directly selling (price, offer, urgency, aggressive claims).
Treat each highlighted sentence as a likely drop-off point — the presenter says these are exactly where readers close the tab.
Rewrite those sentences so they stay inside the narrative: integrate the product as the vehicle for the transformation rather than pausing the story to pitch.
Test the fix: after the reader has passed the product introduction, they should still feel as though they have not yet been sold to.
caveats: The source frames this as a hard rule but is one practitioner's method; some offers legitimately need clearer selling earlier (e.g. price-sensitive, high-intent traffic).
If you sell via native or taboola ads, the source suggests shorter copy with more repeated CTAs, so apply the audit within that structure.

cards.title: Write the After State First, Then Work Backwards
cards.summary: Define the customer's desired future life in vivid detail first, then reverse-engineer the before-state pain so the contrast is visceral.
cards.use_when: When structuring the transformation arc of an advertorial, PDP story block, or landing page for a solution-style product.
steps: Write the after state: what does the customer's life look like once the problem is completely solved? The presenter's example: 'I could finally play tennis again — three games in a row after three years.'
Spend more time on the before state than feels comfortable; agitate the pain of the current situation (can't play tennis, frustrated, tried everything).
Reverse-engineer the narrative: starting from the after state, build the sequence that gets them there.
Insert the product only as the vehicle for the transformation, never as the hero.
Close the loop so the reader's stated perceived value is actually paid off by the end.
Success test: if the reader finishes the advertorial feeling different — with hope — than when they started, the transformation arc worked.
caveats: This is a copy structure, not a guarantee of results; the source gives no performance data.
The tennis/after-state example is illustrative, not a documented case result.

cards.title: Use the Full Storytelling Sequence for a Pre-Lander
cards.summary: A repeatable advertorial structure: benefit headline, mirror, agitate, failed solutions, unique mechanism, social proof, transformation, soft CTA.
cards.use_when: When outlining a pre-lander or advertorial from scratch and deciding the order of sections.
steps: Headline: target the specific persona and include the problem plus transformation, keeping it stupid simple (e.g. 'Woman, 72, how I got rid of knee pain after 3 years').
Hero image: show the transformation side-by-side — problem state (grabbing the knee) versus result state.
Introduction: mirror the reader by describing their problem clearly.
Agitate: make the problem feel bigger in the reader's mind.
List failed solutions they've already tried, so they feel understood.
Introduce the Unique Mechanism — this is what creates hope for a problem they haven't solved in years.
Add social proof (other people who used the mechanism) and reveal the transformation.
Soft CTA: 'Check availability' rather than 'Buy now', with product named only as the thing the doctor asked where to get.
caveats: Presented as a practitioner's template for health/wellness advertorials; adapt the length and section order to your vertical.
The exact section count isn't fixed — the source frames this as his own structure, not a universal requirement.

cards.title: Name the Unique Mechanism So Readers Can Repeat It
cards.summary: Give the product's mechanism a scientific-sounding name and frame it so the reader feels smart enough to retell it at a party.
cards.use_when: When introducing the mechanism that explains how your product works inside an advertorial or landing page.
steps: Choose a specific, impressive-sounding name for the mechanism — the source's example is 'Rheumatoid Trauma Protocol (RTP)'.
Explain it simply enough that a non-expert can repeat it in one or two sentences.
Frame the explanation around the reader telling someone else: 'Did you know this exists?' — the goal is that they retell their discovery to a friend with the same problem.
Position the mechanism as the hope-bringer, after agitation and failed solutions, so it lands as relief.
Use the mechanism in social proof and transformation sections so the name is repeated and remembered.
caveats: The source names 'RTP' as an invented illustrative example, not a real protocol — do not imply scientific validity your product doesn't have.
Naming is one practitioner's 'cocktail party' heuristic; there's no data here on whether naming alone improves conversion.

cards.title: Soft-Sell: Weave the Product Into the Narrative Without Breaking Story
cards.summary: Integrate the product through a character's voice (e.g. a doctor asking where to get it) instead of switching into hard-sales copy.
cards.use_when: When the advertorial needs to mention the product or where to obtain it without jarring the reader out of the story.
steps: Do not pause the narrative to pitch. The source warns that every pitch sentence is a tab-close point.
Put the product in someone else's mouth: 'My doctor was so impressed he asked where to get it' — this keeps the story intact while communicating credibility and availability.
Keep price and aggressive discount language out of the advertorial; the presenter explicitly says don't say 'buy it here for $50 off'.
Use 'Check availability' as the action, not 'Buy now'.
Add a short author bio beneath the CTA ('loves to play tennis in her free time') because people buy from people — the source says to keep this personal and brief.
caveats: This is the presenter's health/wellness advertorial playbook; some categories or compliance environments require explicit pricing or disclaimers.
If running native/paid taboola-style placement, the source suggests shortening copy and adding more CTAs, which changes how much soft-sell you can sustain.

cards.title: Delay the Sticky CTA Until After the Product Is Introduced
cards.summary: The sticky 'Check Availability' button should only appear once the reader has scrolled past the point where the product is introduced.
cards.use_when: When implementing the sticky/scroll-triggered CTA on an advertorial or long-form landing page.
steps: Map where in the copy the product is first introduced.
Set the sticky CTA to appear only after the reader scrolls past that introduction point — not at the top, not at 50%.
The reasoning: before product awareness, showing a buy/check-availability button before the reader knows what the product is creates friction and loses people.
Place supporting microcopy directly above the button (e.g. 'Click the button below to check availability') to nudge the click.
Re-test the trigger point if you change the page structure, since the product introduction may move.
caveats: This is a UX rule of thumb from one practitioner, not a benchmarked result; test per page and traffic source.
Short native/paid pages with multiple CTAs may need different trigger logic.

cards.title: Reinforce Copy with Photorealistic, Paragraph-Matched Images
cards.summary: Every image should visually confirm the paragraph above it, using amateur 'phone-photo' style rather than polished stock.
cards.use_when: When selecting or briefing images for an advertorial, pre-lander, or story-style landing page.
steps: Place the image immediately after the text it supports, so readers finishing a paragraph find the visual confirmation.
Match the image content exactly to the preceding claim — 'show, don't tell' — an incongruent image creates friction the source says will likely make the reader leave.
Use photorealistic, amateur-style imagery as though someone pulled out their phone and took it, because the advertorial reads as a real story/article.
For the hero, use a before/after or problem/result transformation image rather than an abstract product shot.
Check all images against the copy in a final pass and remove any that contradict or distract from the paragraph.
caveats: The source frames this for advertorials that read as editorial stories; standard PDP or brand pages may use different image conventions.
No measured data is given — this is a practitioner's rule of thumb.

cards.title: Apply the Ad-to-Page Congruency Principle Across the Funnel
cards.summary: Carry the same persona, hook, problem and promise from ad creative into the advertorial headline and body through to the product page.
cards.use_when: When planning a paid-traffic funnel (ad → pre-lander → PDP) for a specific segment.
steps: Write the ad around one specific reader persona and their stated problem, not a general audience.
Repeat the same persona and promise in the advertorial headline (e.g. 'Woman, 72, finally free from knee pain after 3 years').
Keep the same person, problem, and duration in the advertorial narrative — no widening to a generic audience.
On the product page, talk about the solution for that same persona and problem duration ('knee pain for women 72 who've had it 3 years').
If any step in the chain drifts to a wider audience, the reader feels less spoken to and the mirror breaks.
caveats: The source notes ad-to-page congruency scaling rules belong to a different discipline (MEA); this card covers only the advertorial-level principle.
The source's examples are health/wellness supplements and braces; adapt personas to your category.

cards.title: Write a Benefit-Driven Advertorial Headline Template
cards.summary: Structure the headline around the exact persona, the problem, and the transformation, using the value equation, kept deliberately simple.
cards.use_when: When drafting the headline for an advertorial, pre-lander, or VSL that runs from paid traffic.
steps: Name the target persona precisely in the headline (e.g. 'Woman, 72').
State the problem and how long they've lived with it ('knee pain for 3 years'), which is the reader's perceived value.
State or imply the transformation ('how I got rid of...'), optionally using the value-equation frame the source references.
Consider a mini-story headline variant: 'Last week, a woman, 72, came into my clinic and finally got rid of her knee pain after 3 years.'
Keep it 'stupid simple' so readers immediately understand what the piece is about.
caveats: The source mentions the value equation but does not detail it — look it up separately if you want to apply it.
Headline examples are illustrative, not tested results.
